bend.verb type: action — dynamic throughout, whether you curve the wire, lean over, or stretch a rule. No linking use; *be bent on winning* is the participle as a predicate adjective, not a copular *bend*.
bend.transitivity: **both** — transitive when you do the curving (*bend the wire*, *bend the rules*, *bend the department to her will*), intransitive when you or the road do the bending (*she bends down*, *the road bends*, *he would not bend to pressure*).
bend.passive: **yes** in the transitive senses — *the coat hanger was bent into a hook*, *the curfew was bent for the seniors*. No passive of the intransitive uses: ✗ *down was bent by her*, ✗ *the road is bent past the mill* (in that reading).

blend.verb type: action — dynamic in every sense, from mixing batter to a newcomer disappearing into a crowd.
blend.transitivity: **both** — transitive when you do the mixing (*blend the butter and the sugar*, *the distillery blended eleven barrels*), intransitive when things merge on their own or someone *blends in* (*their accents have blended*, *he blended in with the crowd*).
blend.passive: **yes** in the transitive senses — *the paint was blended on a scrap of cardboard*, *eleven barrels were blended before bottling*. No passive of *blend in* or the merging sense: ✗ *the crowd was blended in with by him*.

build.verb type: action — dynamic, whether the object is a house, a career, or a case. Never linking and never stative; it always names work or growth over time.
build.transitivity: **both** — transitive in the constructing and developing senses (*they build forty houses a year*, *she builds her arguments one fact at a time*), intransitive when something grows on its own (*pressure builds*, *the tension built through the third act*).
build.passive: **yes**, and very common — *the whole case was built on a single witness*, *the cabinets are built into the wall*. Note the physique sense is passive-only, with no active behind it: *he is built like a linebacker* but ✗ *he builds like a linebacker*.

gild.verb type: action — dynamic: applying gold leaf, or putting a flattering finish on something ordinary. The adjective *gilded* (*the Gilded Age*) is the participle, not a separate class.
gild.transitivity: **transitive** in both senses, and the object is obligatory — *gild the dome*, *gild the lily*. ✗ *Craftsmen gild every fifty years* needs its object.
gild.passive: **yes** — *the capitol dome is gilded about every fifty years*, *a very ordinary hotel was gilded by the brochure*. The perfect passive is ordinary too: *the lettering has been gilded*.

gird.verb type: action — dynamic, elevated in register: bracing yourself for something hard, or belting and encircling in the literal sense.
gird.transitivity: **both** — intransitive or reflexive in the living sense (*retailers gird for the holidays*, *the mayor girded himself for a fight*), transitive in *gird your loins* and the literal encircling (*stone walls had girded the town*).
gird.passive: **restricted** — natural only in the literal encircling sense, and mostly as the short participle: *the island is girt by coral*, *the town was girded by stone walls*. No passive of *gird for*: ✗ *the holidays are girded for*.

lend.verb type: action — dynamic in all senses, even the figurative *lend weight* and *lend an ear*, where nothing physically changes hands.
lend.transitivity: **ditransitive** in the core sense — two objects with no preposition (*lend me twenty dollars*), or one object plus *to* (*she lent the book to a friend*). Also plainly **transitive** in *lend weight*, and **intransitive** in the banking sense: *banks lend at whatever rate the market will bear*.
lend.passive: **yes**, with either object as subject — *the painting had been lent to Chicago*, *he was lent a car for the weekend*. The reflexive *lend itself to* has no passive: ✗ *the novel is lent itself to a two-hour film*.

misspend.verb type: action — dynamic, the *mis-* judgment version of *spend*: money or years put to the wrong use.
misspend.transitivity: **transitive**, object obligatory — *misspend a windfall*, *misspent the entire grant*, *has misspent most of his twenties*. ✗ *The council misspent* is incomplete.
misspend.passive: **yes** — *the entire grant was misspent on consultants*, *money meant for scholarships has been misspent*. In practice you meet the bare participle as an adjective far more often: *a misspent youth*.

outspend.verb type: action — dynamic and comparative: it measures your spending against a rival's.
outspend.transitivity: **transitive**, and the object is obligatory and must be the rival — *her opponent outspent her by two million*. ✗ *We outspent our budget* is the wrong verb; that is *overspend*.
outspend.passive: **yes**, and the passive is at least as common as the active in political and business reporting — *the startup was outspent from the first quarter on*, *being badly outspent did not hurt her*.

overbuild.verb type: action — dynamic: putting up more construction than a place needs, or engineering something far past the required strength.
overbuild.transitivity: **both** — transitive with the place or market as object (*the city overbuilt its downtown*, *Miami has overbuilt its condo market*), intransitive with no object at all (*developers overbuild whenever credit gets cheap*).
overbuild.passive: **yes** in the transitive sense — *the downtown was badly overbuilt in the 1980s*, *the frame had been overbuilt on purpose*. In *the bridge is famously overbuilt* the participle has gone adjectival rather than passive.

overspend.verb type: action — dynamic, measured against your own budget rather than a rival's (that is *outspend*).
overspend.transitivity: **both** — the object is optional: *we overspent by four hundred dollars* and *households overspend every December* stand alone, while *the department has overspent its travel budget* takes one.
overspend.passive: **restricted** — grammatical with a budget or line item as subject (*every line item had been overspent by the third quarter*), but American writing far prefers the participle as an adjective: *an overspent budget*, *an overspent account*.

rebuild.verb type: action — dynamic, always with the implication that something was broken or dismantled first — a town, an engine, a roster, a life.
rebuild.transitivity: **both** — transitive in most senses (*they rebuilt the bridge*, *she rebuilt her life*), intransitive in the American sports sense with no object at all: *ownership chose to rebuild*.
rebuild.passive: **yes** — *the engine was rebuilt twice before the car sold*, *the town had been rebuilt almost entirely*. No passive of the sports sense: ✗ *it was rebuilt by ownership* does not mean the roster overhaul.

rend.verb type: action — dynamic and violent, literary throughout; ordinary American speech uses *tear*. Today you meet the *-ing* form as a compound adjective (*heart-rending*) more often than the verb.
rend.transitivity: **transitive** in every documented sense, object obligatory — *rend the sails*, *rent the party in two*, *a scream rent the silence*. ✗ *The scandal has rent* is incomplete.
rend.passive: **restricted** — grammatical and occasionally used (*the alliance was rent beyond repair*, *the family was rent in two by grief*), but it stays literary; in ordinary prose you would say *torn*.

send.verb type: action — dynamic in all senses, from mailing a package to a gust that *sends papers flying*.
send.transitivity: **ditransitive** in the core sense — *send me the file* or *send the file to me* (never ✗ *send to me the file*) — and **transitive** elsewhere, with the object obligatory: ✗ *I sent yesterday*. The *send + object + -ing/adjective* pattern adds a complement: *sent papers flying*.
send.passive: **yes**, with either object as subject — *four reminders have been sent*, *their daughter was sent to school in Vermont*, *the National Guard was sent in*. Even the figurative sense passivizes: *the stock was sent down forty percent*.

spend.verb type: action — dynamic for both money and time, and figuratively for using up force or goodwill. The participle *spent* has become an adjective (*a spent match*, *I'm completely spent*), but that is not a linking use of the verb.
spend.transitivity: **transitive** — the object is normally obligatory (*spend a hundred dollars*, *spend the afternoon*, *spend the night*), though the money object can be left out in economic talk: *Americans are spending less*.
spend.passive: **yes** — *the entire budget has been spent*, *most of its force had been spent before landfall*. The time sense passivizes naturally too: *the whole afternoon was spent at the DMV*.

unbend.verb type: action — dynamic: straightening something bent, or a stiff person loosening up. Watch the *-ing* form, which has gone adjectival in the opposite direction — *an unbending judge* will not yield at all.
unbend.transitivity: **both** — transitive on physical objects (*unbend the paper clip*, *he unbent the hook*), intransitive both figuratively (*she rarely unbends in front of strangers*) and physically (*he unbent from the garden bed*).
unbend.passive: **restricted** — grammatical in the physical transitive sense but rare, and the participle usually turns up bare: *the wire, once unbent, would not hold its shape*. No passive of the relaxing sense: ✗ *he was unbent since he retired*.

wend.verb type: action — dynamic and archaic, alive almost only in the fossil phrase *wend one's way*; also of a road or stream following a winding course.
wend.transitivity: **both** — technically transitive in *wend one's way*, but the object is fixed and reflexive (*we wended our way through the market*), never free; **intransitive** of a route: *the trail wends along the ridge*.
wend.passive: **no** — the only object is the fixed *one's way*, which cannot become a subject: ✗ *their way was wended through the market*. The winding-course sense is intransitive and has no passive at all.
